newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's July CPI seen rising 1.0 to 1.2 percent.
newsitem.headline: Israel's July CPI seen rising 1.0 to 1.2 percent.

text.p: Israel's July consumer price index (CPI), to be released on Friday, will post a rise of 1.0 to 1.2 percent, economists forecast on Thursday.
This follows a larger-than-expected increase of 1.1 percent in June. In July 1996 the CPI grew by only 0.3 percent.
An increase of 1.0 percent would bring inflation in the past 12 months to 9.2 percent. The government set a 1997 inflation target of seven to 10 percent.
Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, forecast a rise of 1.1 to 1.2 percent in July.

"It's pretty bad and will lead to an interest rate increase of 0.3 to 0.5 percentage point at the end of the month," Katz said. "July is seasonally very low with a drop in fruit and vegetable prices and end of season clothing sales."
The central bank's key lending rate stands at 12.7 percent.
Bank Hapoalim chief economist Ptachia Bar Shavit estimates July's CPI rose 1.0 percent. He said such a rise increases the chance of an interest rate hike of up to 0.5 percentage point.
"Half of that (CPI) is because of housing," he said.
Housing prices, which are linked to the dollar, rose following a 2.5 percent depreciation of the shekel as well as the dollar's strengthening against other currencies abroad.
Katz said stronger demand for housing led to an increase in prices beyond the linkage to the dollar.

"Possibly people were concerned about the dollar's rise and rushed to close deals before a further depreciation. But it could also be cyclical after a year in which housing demand was very low and people postponed purchases," Katz said.
Hezy Gutman, chief economist at the First International Bank of Israel, forecast a 1.1 percent rise in July's CPI.
He said higher housing prices were a key factor in the sharp rise in June's CPI, which was not affected by the exchange rate.
"We are seeing signs of a revival in the housing market. There is a decline in supply, housing starts are down. We are going from surplus supply to surplus demand," he said.
A revival in the Tel Aviv stock market has helped relieve a credit crunch, enabling builders to once again turn to the bourse as a source of capital, he added.
Imports priced in dollars will also become more expensive due to the dollar's rise.

The dollar's strength against currencies such as the mark and yen could have a slightly positive effect on the CPI in relation to items such as cars and consumer electronics imported from Europe and Japan, Gutman said.
"But overall the dollar's strengthening is not good for inflation," he added.
Most economists believe inflation will end the year just below or right around 10 percent.
"We're still looking at slightly under 10 percent. I would say a lot depends on external factors such as what happens to the dollar in world markets," Katz said.
"This still is a small economy and linkage to the dollar exchange rate is still very high."
Bank Hapoalim originally forecast inflation of 8.5 percent in 1997. "Now we are at 9.5 or 9.6 percent," Bar Shavit said.

Gutman predicts inflation will end the year at 9.5 to 10 percent. "If this is the trend in inflation it's pretty clear what the Bank of Israel governor will do. He won't have a choice but to raise interest rates," Gutman said.

"Almost every parameter justifies a rate hike -- the last two CPIs, money supply growth, higher inflationary expectations (in the capital markets) and even the economic slowdown, which is not worsening."
